 Print Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has addressed the question over the tech giant’s massive new buyout program and whether this is a sign of upcoming AI-driven layoffs, explaining that the company is reshaping how its teams work rather than simply shrinking its headcount. Speaking after Microsoft rolled out a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) to roughly 60,000 workers, which is more than a quarter of its global staff—Nadella emphasized that the future of the company will look noticeably different in terms of team sizes and daily workflows. “It’s a very important question. Let’s acknowledge that there is going to be plenty of opportunity going forward. The shape of that opportunity may be different,” Nadella said, adding, “The shape of what this new thing looks like is going to be different than what it was before: team sizes and team workflows.” While Nadella stressed that he wants all 200,000-plus Microsoft employees to grow and flourish, he noted that the workforce “will have to be configured in different ways. ” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella : ‘Vote with your feet’
 According to the CEO, the voluntary buyout is designed to give employees control over their careers as the company evolves, especially for those sitting in units that have been slow to adapt. “This voluntary thing was mostly about letting everybody have more agency to get themselves into places that make sense for their economic opportunity long term. That's, I think, the key thing. I don't want to be stuck in a team that's not transforming, even inside of Microsoft. Let's face it. It's not like I can sit here and say every part of Microsoft has really got the memo," Nadella explained at The Pragmatic Engineer podcast. He added that employees who feel professionally stuck now have the option to leave on good terms, though he encouraged them to explore internal transfers first. “If you're in a team where you feel stuck professionally, you can vote with your feet. I don't want you to, because quite frankly there are many places you can go inside of Microsoft itself. I wish I could just sit here and say it'll all be the same. I cannot. And this is one of those places where I want to be as transparent about the change,” Nadella said. What was Microsoft’s buyout offer
 Chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the Voluntary Exit Offer in a memo to staff, framing it as a chance for employees already considering a move outside Microsoft to exit now with financial backing and career support. The offer applies to eligible staff at internal level 70 and below, which is a group that includes roles up to general managers and some vice presidents, across just four countries: The US, Canada, The UK and India. Unlike Microsoft’s spring retirement buyout, this offer has no age or tenure minimums and job performance is not a factor. Eligible workers have until the first week of December to decide, with departures set for the end of the year. The buyout terms match Microsoft’s standard severance package. During US layoffs earlier this year, severance included at least 60 days of base pay on the payroll and up to 39 weeks of base pay depending on seniority and tenure – giving employees at level 64 and below one week of base pay per six months of service, and those at levels 65 to 67 two weeks per six months.  The VEO also covers continued stock vesting, career transition help, and healthcare coverage for a fixed period. Unlike the earlier retirement program, however, it does not include extended healthcare benefits. Individual terms are being sent via email to eligible staff, including those in India. This marks Microsoft’s second major buyout push in 2026 following waves of layoffs over the past two years. In 2025 cuts, Microsoft eliminated more than 15,000 jobs. This year, the company launched its first-ever Voluntary Retirement Program for about 8,750 US staff (senior director level and below) whose age and years of service totaled at least 70. Microsoft laid off 4,800 workers (around 2% of its workforce) in July, hitting Xbox and commercial sales hardest, followed by hundreds more cuts in September.
